conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you so much for making time for this today. My name is Dr. Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in the emotional changes that can come after childbirth, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported.

In front of us we have the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting or your strength; it’s just a way for us to spot anything that might benefit from extra care, whether that’s low mood, anxiety, or even thoughts of self-harm.

Everything you share stays between you and the clinical team unless you tell me something that makes us worry about your immediate safety. We’ll talk through each question one at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about perfect wording. If any question feels tough, we can pause or come back to it.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt harder to do lately?

[offering a small, tired smile]  
I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes that silly face with the burp cloth on his head—but it doesn’t come as easily. Mostly I’m just… flat. Even when I recognize something’s funny, the laugh feels kind of half-hearted, like I’m going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod, eyes on my lap]

Mostly yes, I guess… I can still laugh, especially when the baby does that little startled face or when my partner tries to dance with the vacuum. But the laugh feels lighter than it used to—like it fades fast and I’m right back to feeling blank. So I’d say “yes,” just not with the same heart I had before.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugging slightly, voice quiet]

I do look forward to some things—like my mom coming over tomorrow or the first cup of coffee in the morning—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. It’s more… “oh, that’ll be nice,” and then I worry I won’t even enjoy it when it happens.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[glancing down at my hands, voice soft]

Yeah... I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby wouldn't settle for almost an hour and I kept thinking, "What am I doing wrong? Maybe I'm not feeding him right, or maybe I missed some cue." Even little things—like spilling a bit of pumped milk—make me feel like I messed up big time, even though I know accidents happen.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[lightly twisting the edge of my cardigan]

A few times a day I’ll suddenly feel my heart race—like when the baby’s snoring pattern changes or when I can’t remember if I sterilised the dummy. I’ll tell myself it’s nothing serious, take a breath, and calm down within a few minutes, but it pops up out of nowhere maybe once or twice daily.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[pressing my lips together, then exhaling]

Not really panicky, no. I get those quick “what-if” flutters, but they don’t turn into a full scared feeling. I can talk myself down pretty fast, so I wouldn’t say I’ve been truly frightened without a reason—just the little worry spikes that pass.
Things have been getting on top of me

[shoulders rise in a small shrug]

Sometimes, yeah. Like when the laundry pile looks bigger than the bassinet and the baby wants to cluster-feed for an hour, I feel this wave of “I can’t keep up.” I usually manage—my sister came over and helped fold clothes yesterday—but every so often it feels as though the day is running me instead of the other way around.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[shaking my head slowly]

No, it hasn’t been that bad. I do lie awake some nights thinking over everything I need to do, but I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy that I can’t sleep. Once I drift off I’m usually out for a few hours until the baby wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes drop to the floor, voice small]

Yeah… I do feel that way some days. Not all day—there are bright moments—but a kind of heavy sadness keeps coming back, especially in the late afternoon when the house is quiet and I’m just sitting there feeding. I’ll tear up for no clear reason, then feel guilty for feeling sad when I “should” be grateful.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[pressing my lips together, eyes sting a little]

I’ve cried… maybe twice this week. Not sobbing all day—just sudden tears when I couldn’t get the baby to latch right away and felt like I was failing him. It passes pretty quickly, but yeah, those moments hit me out of nowhere and leave me feeling shaky for a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shaking my head quickly]

No—never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk post-delivery, first child, breastfeeding, partner and family support available.

Responses to EPDS-equivalent items:

Affect / Mood  
– Endorses recurrent “heavy” sadness most days, worse late afternoon, associated with tearfulness (Q8, Q9).  
– Reports diminished emotional return from previously enjoyable activities; laughter described as “lighter” and “fading fast” (Q1, Q2).

Cognition / Self-appraisal  
– Frequent self-blame over routine infant-care mishaps; labels self as “failing” (Q3).  
– Guilt about feeling sad when “should be grateful” (Q8).

Anxiety  
– Episodic, unprovoked heart-racing 1–2× daily, quickly self-resolved; content focuses on infant safety (Q4).  
– Denies full panic attacks or persistent panic-level fear (Q5).

Functional impact  
– “Wave of ‘I can’t keep up’” amid household tasks; describes day “running me” (Q6).  
– Sleep onset occasionally delayed by rumination; returns to sleep after infant feeds (Q7).

Safety  
– Explicitly denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No current suicidal ideation reported.

Risk factors for perinatal mood/anxiety disorder  
✓ Persistent sad mood, anhedonia, crying spells  
✓ Excessive guilt / self-criticism  
✓ Physiological anxiety symptoms without external trigger  
✓ Subjective sense of being overwhelmed / diminished coping  
✓ No self-harm ideation at present

Screening impression  
Patient reports multiple symptoms consistent with mild–moderate postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety. Frequency and distress appear above “baby blues” threshold; denies functional impairment in infant care but acknowledges emotional burden. Continue monitoring; consider formal assessment (EPDS score, clinical interview) and discussion of supports/interventions.
